claims.text: In single-phase disordered high-entropy alloys, superconductivity is primarily governed by controlled changes in local lattice distortion.
Systematic substitution of one alloying element can induce controlled changes in local lattice distortion.
Substitution-induced local lattice distortions modulate electron-phonon coupling.
At an optimal substitution level, changes in electron count and local disorder enhance superconducting pairing interactions.
Enhanced pairing interactions at the optimal substitution level increase Tc relative to the unmodified alloy.
Pair-breaking caused by excessive substitution lowers Tc.
Local lattice distortions modify the phonon density of states.
Local lattice distortions modify the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the phonon and electronic densities of states affect electron-phonon coupling strength.
Substitution-driven enhancement of electron-phonon coupling favors Cooper-pair formation.
Excessive substitution can cause lattice instability.
Tc will vary non-monotonically across the substitution series.
A moderate substitution level will increase Tc relative to the unmodified baseline alloy.
Further substitution beyond the moderate level will decrease Tc.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase disordered solid solution.
Phase separation, significant ordering, or compositional inhomogeneity may prevent the predicted Tc enhancement.
The optimal substitution level and magnitude of electron-phonon-coupling changes depend on the specific alloy system.

contradictions.description: Phase separation or significant ordering is defined as placing the material outside the mechanism's applicability boundary, but the falsification rule also treats observing either condition as falsifying the mechanism. An out-of-domain sample cannot by itself decisively falsify a hypothesis restricted to single-phase disordered alloys.
